newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia settles down after weekend violence.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia settles down after weekend violence.

text.p: Calm had returned to areas of Indonesia's main island of Java hit by a fresh bout of pre-election violence between rival political groups over the weekend, the national police said on Monday.
"From the view of the national police, it's safe and under control," national police spokesman Brigadier-General Nurfaizi told Reuters in Jakarta.

Supporters of the ruling Golkar and the minority Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) clashed in major centres on Java, including the capital Jakarta and the ancient city of Yogyakarta on the final weekend of campaigning before the May 29 elections.

Despite the violent confrontations, with thousands of supporters of the two parties hurling stones and other projectiles at each other as police and troops moved to keep them apart, there were no immediate reports of casualties or arrests.
Shops and businesses were open on Monday and streets were jammed with traffic as usual.
"There is nothing to worry about as the situation has been controlled and the activities of the community can continue as usual," Nurfaizi said.
Financial markets were cautious, with Jakarta stocks opening lower after the weekend violence, but dealers and brokers said share-price movements were within acceptable limits.

"We see it very much as a very, very short term impact, and really as of next Friday (when the campaign ends) all bets are on again," said Stephen Doe, director of research with Asia Equities Jasereh brokerage.
There is a five-day cooling off period between the end of the election campaign and polling day when 125 million people in the world's fourth most populous country will be eligible to vote.

The only other party legally entitled to contest the election, the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), was campaigning in Java on Monday. But the party has been badly split since the ouster of its former leader Megawati Sukarnoputri last year and has been drawing mediocre support.
The three parties issued a statement on Sunday night saying they would halt all mass public rallies in Jakarta for the rest of the campaign.
In the central Java city of Yogyakarta, anti-riot police broke up a demonstration by more than 500 university students at about midnight on Sunday, witnesses said.
They said the students hurled stones and chanted slogans against Golkar following unconfirmed reports that three of their colleagues were attacked by supporters of the ruling party.
In Bantul, south of Yogyakarta, Golkar supporters were reported by newspapers to have attacked a mosque on their way home from a campaign rally but no further details were available.
The country's powerful military said the violence was part of a plot to topple long-ruling President Suharto and blamed radicals who it said were linked to the banned Indonesian Communist Party.
Political analysts said, however, that the authorities routinely blamed radicals for violence and any failings in the system.
Golkar's platform stresses social and economic development, while the other parties are emphasising a drive against corruption and the need for more open democracy.
But a senior Asian diplomat said there had been little substance involved in the campaign so far.

"There has been very little in the way of substantive issues involved. You hear criticism against corruption and collusion, but nobody can really pin down the election issues. It has turned out to be a contest for votes, not a contest of substance," the diplomat said.
